questions.q: State the NCERT definition of work simplification and name the two resources it explicitly aims to blend and manage.
questions.a: Work simplification is the conscious seeking of the simplest, easiest, and quickest method of doing work, implying proper blending and management of time and human energy to accomplish more work with given resources or reduce resources for given work. A wrong answer that omits "conscious seeking" or names "money and space" instead of "time and human energy" reveals the student has memorised a generic definition without understanding the specific resource focus of this concept.

questions.q: A student says: "Using a pressure cooker instead of an open pot is a change in hand and body motions because you stir less." Is this correct? Explain why or why not using the three levels of change.
questions.a: This is incorrect. Using a pressure cooker is a Level 2 change (change in equipment used), not Level 1. Level 1 involves only changes in hand/body motions with the SAME tools and product. The pressure cooker is a different equipment that alters the cooking method itself. A student who misclassifies this confuses the boundary between motion improvement (same tools) and equipment substitution (different tools), showing they haven't grasped the "keeping the same work tools and product" condition for Level 1.

questions.q: Your family currently buys whole wheat, takes it to the chakki for grinding, stores the atta in a steel container, and makes rotis daily. Propose ONE specific change at EACH of the three levels that would simplify this work, and explain why each fits its level.
questions.a: Level 1 (motions): Combine trips — bring a month's wheat supply in one chakki visit instead of weekly, eliminating repeated transport motions. Level 2 (equipment/storage): Install a pull-out flour bin at counter height near the rolling board, replacing the steel container on a high shelf, reducing bending and reaching. Level 3 (end product): Switch to multigrain atta (different raw material) or make stuffed parathas instead of plain rotis (different product from same material), reducing the need for separate side dishes. A wrong answer that puts "buying readymade atta" in Level 1 reveals confusion — buying readymade atta changes the raw material (Level 3), not just motions.

questions.q: Compare and contrast "doing all dusting, then all sweeping, then all mopping" (like tasks together) versus "cleaning one room completely before moving to the next" in terms of Level 1 work simplification principles. Which better applies the principle of rhythm and sequence? Justify.
questions.a: "Doing like tasks together" better applies the rhythm and sequence principle. It maintains a consistent body posture (standing, sweeping motion) and tool use (broom) across rooms, reducing motion transitions and mental switching costs. "One room at a time" forces posture changes (dusting high → sweeping low → mopping wet) and tool changes repeatedly, breaking rhythm. A student who claims both are equal misses that rhythm refers to sustained repetitive motion patterns, not just task completion order — this is a specific Level 1 principle about motor pattern efficiency.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "Level 3 changes (changing the end product) are always the most effective for work simplification because they eliminate the most steps." Defend or critique with two concrete examples.
questions.a: Critique: Level 3 is NOT always most effective. Example 1: Switching from home-cooked dal-chawal to ordered takeout (Level 3) eliminates cooking steps but increases cost, reduces nutrition, and may not be sustainable daily — effectiveness depends on context. Example 2: Using a long-handled broom (Level 1) eliminates back strain for a 60-year-old doing daily sweeping — this low-cost motion change has higher daily impact than changing the product. Effectiveness = (time/energy saved) × (frequency) ÷ (cost/disruption). A student who agrees uncritically treats Level 3 as universally superior, ignoring the trade-off triangle of cost, acceptability, and frequency that determines real-world effectiveness.

questions.q: Design a Level 1 + Level 2 combined work simplification plan for "washing and storing school uniforms for a family of three children" that reduces total time by at least 20% without changing the end product (clean, pressed uniforms). List specific changes at each level.
questions.a: Level 1: (a) Sort all uniforms together before washing (one sorting motion vs three), (b) Hang uniforms directly on hangers from the line (eliminates folding + re-hanging), (c) Use a two-bucket system (wash/rinse) to avoid refilling. Level 2: (a) Install a wall-mounted drying rack at standing height near the washing area (eliminates bending to low line), (b) Use a mesh laundry bag for socks/small items (prevents loss, eliminates sorting post-wash), (c) Place ironing board and iron storage at the uniform hanging zone (eliminates carrying). A poor answer that suggests "buy a washing machine" only addresses Level 2 and ignores the no-product-change constraint — it also assumes budget availability, which Level 1 changes don't require.
